confounds: Posting volume differs by label: diagnosed users averaged about 620 retained posts versus 531 for controls, with medians of 391 versus 334; raw post frequencies therefore require per-user normalization.
Explicit depression wording weakened across development folds even though its direction stayed positive, suggesting temporal, source, or cohort drift.
Treatment and psychiatric-care language is affected by healthcare access, stigma, self-disclosure, and annotation/collection practices.
K-pop, LGBTQ+, pronoun, and online-fandom signals may proxy age, gender, identity, community, or platform subculture rather than depression-related semantics.
First-person heuristics can misclassify quotations, lyrics, jokes, sarcasm, advocacy, news, and discussion of relatives or other users.
Generic Portuguese words such as sleep, tiredness, friends, work, school, medication, and loneliness are polysemous and require contextual and persistence checks.
The strong class imbalance means aggregate post totals are not directly comparable; user-level prevalence is the safer primary measure.

negative_results: Unqualified words for sleep, relationships, work/study, future, leisure, and social activity were near-universal; first-person context and persistence were necessary for useful separation.
Positive future language was near ceiling in both groups and had slightly higher raw post share among controls, so it is not a reliable protective or exclusionary signal.
Humor and social/leisure participation remained common among diagnosed users; their presence does not rule out impairment or treatment narratives.
Politics, news, and football had higher raw post shares among controls, but user-level coverage was near-equal or fold-unstable, demonstrating prolific-user and topic-mix confounding.
